# How bacteria copy themselves and change

> *Bacteria change in two ways: through errors in copying their own DNA, and by taking in DNA from
> other bacteria. Both happen at random, and drug use then selects whichever variants survive. That
> sequence explains antimicrobial resistance, and also how a harmless strain can acquire a toxin.*

## Copying the genome {#sec-gen-copy}

A typical bacterium carries one circular chromosome. The chromosome of *Escherichia coli* has about
4.6 million base pairs and some 4,300 genes. Many bacteria also carry **plasmids**: small, circular
DNA molecules that replicate independently and often carry genes the cell can live without, such as
genes for resistance or toxins. Before dividing by binary fission, the cell copies its chromosome,
starting from a single origin and working round the circle in both directions.

Bacteria follow the same central dogma as your cells, with differences that matter clinically.

| Step | Your cells | Bacteria | Why the difference matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Where it happens | Transcription in the nucleus, translation in the cytoplasm | Both in the cytoplasm at the same time: ribosomes start on an mRNA while it is still being made | Gene expression can change within minutes |
| Gene organisation | One gene per mRNA; genes interrupted by introns | Related genes often share one mRNA, as an **operon**; introns are rare | A whole pathway can be switched on at once |
| RNA polymerase | Several polymerases | One core enzyme of a different structure | A target human cells do not share |
| Ribosomes | 80S (40S and 60S subunits) | 70S (30S and 50S subunits) | A major drug target; mitochondria have bacterial-type ribosomes, which explains some drug side effects |
| DNA supercoiling | Human topoisomerases | DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV | A target with no exact human equivalent |

The right-hand column answers the sixth question for the machinery of inheritance. The pharmacology
block names the drugs that use each target.

## Change by mutation {#sec-gen-mutation}

A **mutation** is a change in the DNA sequence. Most arise as copying errors during replication: a
**point mutation** replaces one base with another, while insertions and deletions add or remove bases.
DNA-based microbes make roughly one new mutation for every 300 genomes copied [@drake1991constant].
That rate sounds low, but bacterial populations are large, and resistance to a single drug can often
arise from any one of several different mutations. An infection containing billions of bacteria
usually already contains resistant mutants before treatment begins.

Most mutations are neutral or harmful. A few, by chance, alter the protein a drug acts on so that the
drug binds poorly. Whether the drug is present has no bearing on which mutations occur. Salvador Luria
and Max Delbrück showed this in 1943: the number of resistant bacteria varied widely between parallel
cultures, in the pattern expected if mutants arise at random during growth and not in response to the
selecting agent [@luria1943mutations]. Joshua and Esther Lederberg later showed it directly. Using
replica plating, they picked colonies from a plate that had never been exposed to the selecting agent
and found that they were already resistant [@lederberg1952replica].

Grow the population below, decide whether resistant cells exist yet, then add the drug.

<div data-island="selection-sim" data-src="/diagrams/selection-sim.yml"></div>

The drug made no bacterium resistant. It killed the susceptible cells, and the resistant cells that
were already present grew into the space. This is **selection**. Repeated across many patients and
many courses of treatment, it is how resistance becomes common.

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "bacteria mutate in order to survive the drug"
In one study, 81% of undergraduates agreed that bacteria develop mutations *in order to* become
resistant [@richard2017intuitive]. Bacteria have no way of producing the mutation they need. Mutations
arise at random, and the drug selects the cells that happen to carry a useful one. Stress from some
drugs can raise the overall mutation rate a little, but the mutations remain random with respect to
resistance. A related belief, that the *body* becomes resistant, is held by 62.5% of Singapore
residents [@lim2021singaporekap]. Resistance is a property of bacteria, and resistant bacteria spread
between people.
:::

## Change by gene transfer {#sec-gen-hgt}

Bacteria can also acquire whole genes from other bacteria. This is **horizontal gene transfer**, as
distinct from vertical inheritance from a parent cell. There are three classic routes.

**Transformation** is the uptake of free DNA released by dead cells. Some species, including
*Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Neisseria*, are naturally **competent**: they actively take up DNA from
their surroundings. Transformation was the first route discovered, in the experiment followed by the
case at the end of this chapter.

**Transduction** occurs when a **bacteriophage**, a virus that infects bacteria, packages a piece of
its host's DNA by mistake and injects it into the next bacterium it infects.

**Conjugation** is the transfer of a plasmid from one cell to another through direct contact, usually
through a thin tube called a pilus. The older name "sex pilus" is misleading, because bacteria have no
sexes and conjugation produces no offspring. It copies a plasmid into a neighbouring cell, which can
belong to a different species.

**Transposons** ("jumping genes") move genes within and between DNA molecules. They are DNA segments
that can cut or copy themselves into a new position, for example from the chromosome onto a plasmid,
which can then carry them to another cell. Over time, plasmids and transposons collect several
resistance genes together, so a single transfer can confer resistance to several drugs.

Gene transfer moves virulence genes as well. Clusters of virulence genes acquired together in this way
are called **pathogenicity islands**. Much of the difference between a harmless gut *E. coli* and a
strain that causes bloody diarrhoea lies in genes of this kind.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-vertical-horizontal.yml"></div>

## Bacteriophages: lytic and lysogenic {#sec-gen-phage}

Phages are the most numerous biological entities on Earth. After injecting its genome, a phage
follows one of two paths. In the **lytic cycle**, the phage takes over the cell, makes hundreds of new
phages, and **lyses** (bursts) the cell to release them. In the **lysogenic cycle**, the phage genome
joins the bacterial chromosome as a **prophage** and is copied with it each time the cell divides;
damage to the bacterium's DNA can later switch the prophage into the lytic cycle.

A prophage can change what its host does, which is called **lysogenic conversion**. Several of the
best-known bacterial toxins are encoded by phage genes rather than by the bacterium's own chromosome.

| Toxin | Organism | Effect of lysogenic conversion |
|---|---|---|
| Diphtheria toxin | *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* | Only strains carrying the phage are **toxigenic** (toxin-producing) and cause diphtheria |
| Cholera toxin | *Vibrio cholerae* | The toxin genes arrived on a phage [@waldor1996cholera] |
| Shiga toxins | Some *E. coli*, such as O157:H7 | Phage-borne toxin genes turned a gut commensal into a cause of bloody diarrhoea |
| Pyrogenic exotoxins | *Streptococcus pyogenes* | Phage-borne superantigen genes, behind scarlet fever |

The same species can therefore be harmless or dangerous depending on which phages it carries, which
is the genetic side of the fifth question.

## Resistance: what it is and how it spreads {#sec-gen-resistance}

**Antimicrobial resistance** is the ability of a microbe to grow in the presence of a drug that would
normally inhibit or kill it. Some resistance is **intrinsic**, a property of the whole species: drugs
that act on the cell wall cannot affect *Mycoplasma*, which has no wall. Most clinically important
resistance is **acquired**, by mutation or gene transfer. Whatever its origin, resistance works in one
of four ways.

| Mechanism | How it works | Usual genetic origin |
|---|---|---|
| Destroy or modify the drug | An enzyme breaks the drug down or blocks its active site | Genes on plasmids and transposons |
| Change the target | The drug's target protein is altered so the drug binds poorly | Mutation, or an acquired gene for a different version of the target, as in MRSA ([*Gram-positive cocci*](../microbes/gram-positive-cocci.qmd)) |
| Keep the drug out | Fewer **porins**, the channels in the Gram-negative outer membrane, let less drug in | Mutation |
| Pump the drug out | **Efflux pumps** in the membrane expel the drug | Mutation increasing pump production, or acquired pump genes |

Three consequences follow. Every use of an antimicrobial, in people or in animals, selects resistant
bacteria. Resistance genes on plasmids spread between species, so selection in one organism can create
resistance in another. And resistance often carries a cost: without the drug, resistant bacteria may
grow a little more slowly, which is one reason reducing drug use can help, although many resistance
genes persist for years.

**Antimicrobial stewardship** is the coordinated effort to use antimicrobials only when they are
needed, at the right dose and for the right duration, so that selection is kept to a minimum. Because
selection acts on populations, stewardship depends on every prescriber, not on infection specialists
alone. The pharmacology block covers the drugs.
